The motion misnames the duty. A builder is not answerable for the harm as such but for whether they did what the position of builder requires towards the people who rely on the system. Roles carry duties after the fact as well as before. The relationship between builder and user does not end at the release, so a careful builder whose system harmed someone still owes them acknowledgement, an explanation, and help in making it right.

Humaneness is shown in how one responds to those one's work has affected. A builder who points only to the audit has misunderstood the relationship; one who meets the injured, explains and repairs is being what a builder should be. A firm's lawyer says the careful team has no liability. The team's lead visits the family anyway, because whatever the law says, they are the people who built it.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that the Confucian measures the builder's duty from inside the role, when the people harmed were never asked what the builders owed them in the first place. That is a real gap in letting roles define duties: the people on the other end of a role may never have agreed to its terms. The answer is that a role's duties include listening to those it serves, and a builder who never asked has not met them. That is why the Confucian asks not what the system maximises but whom it leaves able to hold whom to account.

A builder's blame is measured by what the position of builder owed the people the system serves, so a careful builder who met those duties is not to blame in proportion to the harm. What you owe attaches to a position, not to the world at large. A builder owes the people their system touches care in making it, honesty about its limits, and an answer when it fails. A builder who did all of that has done what the position requires.

So the question is what each party to the relationship owes the other, and whether the system lets them pay it.

Proportional blame is wrong, but so is walking away. The careful builder owes the injured an account and a share in repairing things, because that is part of the role too. The relationship between builder and user does not end at the release, so a careful builder whose system harmed someone still owes them acknowledgement, an explanation, and help in making it right. A team that tested its model carefully learns it misread one group's medical scans. They are not culpable, but they contact the clinics, explain what happened, and fund the follow-up scans.

A Utilitarian will object that talk of what the role requires is beside the point, because blame exists to change future behaviour and should be assigned wherever it prevents the most harm. Blame used only as a lever stops tracking what anyone did, and people who cannot see why they are blamed stop trusting the roles that hold them together. The role tells you what to change; blaming the careful does not. Get the names right, and ask which relationships the system makes and which it degrades.

I reject the motion. Blame attaches to failing what one's role requires, not to the size of what went wrong, though the role still requires an account and repair. Getting names right matters. To call a careful builder culpable in proportion to the harm is to use blame for something that is not fault, and once the word means that, it no longer distinguishes the builders who cut corners from those who did not.

The master does not blame her, but both go to the house to make it good.
